speech1.title: Speech perception: from sound to categories
paragraphs: **Speech perception** turns changing sound into a linguistic message. The sound reaching the ear is continuous, but the words recognized through it contain distinctions such as /b/ versus /p/.
The central question is how the listener extracts stable categories from variable input. Formants, synthetic speech, and labeling and discrimination experiments make that question testable.

speech1.title: A stable message in a variable signal
paragraphs: A speech waveform contains overlapping movements of the vocal tract rather than neatly separated letters. The spectrogram spreads this signal across time and frequency, making some of its structure visible.

Different speakers can express the same message with very different voices. Vocal-tract anatomy, speaking rate, and surrounding sounds change the physical input without necessarily changing the words.
Recognition therefore requires more than matching the sound to one exact recording. The listener must preserve differences that distinguish linguistic categories while tolerating other variation.

speech1.title: From an analog signal to a symbolic representation
paragraphs: An **analog signal** varies continuously: a frequency or a timing interval can change by small amounts. A **symbolic representation** groups that variation into units the language system can use, such as a phoneme.

**Categorical perception** is one proposed bridge between these descriptions. Several physically different sounds may receive the same label, while a small change near a boundary produces a different label.
The proposed benefit is a stable input to later language processes. Whether the system completely discards fine acoustic detail is a separate question from whether its final labels look categorical.

speech1.title: Formants reflect the shape of the vocal tract
paragraphs: **Formants** are resonant frequency regions amplified by the vocal tract. Changing the shape of the tract changes which frequencies are emphasized in the outgoing sound.
The vocal-tract drawings pair different articulatory shapes with different resonance patterns. The relationship is lawful: the shape acts as a filter rather than adding an arbitrary linguistic label.
A **formant transition** is a movement in one of these resonances over time. A steady formant helps characterize a vowel; a transition can reveal the articulatory movement into that vowel.

speech1.title: Reading vowel spectrograms
paragraphs: A **spectrogram** places time horizontally and frequency vertically. Dark bands show concentrations of acoustic energy; the formants are prominent bands that differ across the listed vowels.

Compare the vowels in bead, bid, bade, bed, and bad, then the remaining examples. Their identity changes with the pattern of resonances, rather than with the presence of a single universal vowel frequency.
F1 and F2 provide a useful description of these contrasts. Their combination matters: hearing one band in isolation would throw away part of the vowel pattern.

speech1.title: The /u/ example: first and second formants
paragraphs: The /u/ recording has a low first formant, around 300 Hz, and a low second formant, around 900 Hz. These are two resonances of the same vowel, not two different spoken sounds.
The waveform shows pressure variation over time; the spectrogram below it shows where energy is concentrated in frequency. The cursor identifies F1 within that display.
This example gives a concrete starting point for synthesis: keep the source constant, change selected resonance frequencies, and hear how the vowel changes.

speech1.title: Tracking formants in Praat
paragraphs: The automatic tracks estimate the changing formant frequencies through the recording. Five tracks are identified. The first three are usually important for phonemic processing, although the demonstration concentrates on the first two.
F1 is the lowest formant, F2 is the next, and higher numbers refer to higher resonances. These labels specify their order, not separate speakers or successive syllables.
Tracking the resonances makes it possible to describe a vowel with a small set of changing acoustic properties and then manipulate those properties deliberately.

speech1.title: Separating the source from the filter
paragraphs: The **source** is the sound that the vocal tract filters. Removing the estimated filter from the recording leaves a more buzz-like signal with less of the original vowel quality.
The extraction uses the formant pattern to estimate what the tract contributed. The result is an approximate source that can be sent through different filters.

This separates two causes of the final sound: the excitation that supplies energy and the resonances that shape its spectrum. Changing the second while holding the first fixed tests the contribution of the filter.

speech1.title: Changing the filter while keeping the source
paragraphs: The first filter approximates the resonances of the original recording. Another raises F1, and another raises F2 more substantially. Each manipulation changes which frequencies receive amplification.
Because the source is held fixed, a resulting vowel difference can be traced to the filter change. Raising F1 and raising F2 are distinct manipulations, even though both alter vowel quality.
The displays represent filters through time. They are instructions for shaping the source, rather than three naturally recorded speakers whose voices differ in many uncontrolled ways.

speech1.title: Recombining source and filter
paragraphs: Applying each filter to the same source produces a new sound. The resulting spectrograms show how the resonance pattern changes when a selected formant is moved.
The important comparison is between a constant source and different filters. A changed vowel quality shows that vocal-tract resonance patterns are sufficient to alter what vowel the listener hears.
This is a controlled demonstration of **source–filter synthesis**: manipulate a defined acoustic cause, then compare both the physical output and its perceptual identity.

speech1.title: Vowel space contains distributions
paragraphs: A **vowel space** represents vowels using formant values, commonly F1 and F2. Each vowel occupies a region containing many productions, rather than one exact pair of frequencies.
Anatomy, rate, and neighboring phones move a production within this space. Regions can overlap, so a measured formant value does not always uniquely identify a vowel.
Steady formants can still generate recognizable approximations. The listener's task is to recognize useful structure in variable distributions rather than demand physically identical examples.

speech1.title: The pattern playback synthesizer
paragraphs: The **pattern playback** device converts a visible acoustic pattern into a speech-like sound. A drawn pattern specifies how energy should be distributed over frequency and time.
Its role is to let researchers control the stimulus instead of relying only on naturally spoken syllables. A chosen transition can be altered while other portions of the pattern remain constant.
Synthetic speech makes a causal question possible: when just one acoustic property changes, does perceived phoneme identity change smoothly or in categories?

speech1.title: Stop consonants and formant transitions
paragraphs: The stop consonants /b/, /d/, and /g/ involve different places of closure. Their audible release into a vowel contains rapidly changing formant information as the articulators move.
Liberman and colleagues used synthetic patterns to reproduce these transitions. The listener hears a syllable even though the researcher can specify the transition independently.
The critical cue is therefore not only a steady vowel resonance. The direction and starting position of a transition can help distinguish consonants leading into a similar vowel.

speech1.title: Constructing an evenly spaced speech continuum
paragraphs: F1 stays constant while the starting frequency of F2 changes in equal steps. This creates a **continuum**: adjacent stimuli differ physically by the same amount.
Toward one region listeners hear /b/, in another /d/, and toward the other end /g/. The equal physical spacing lets perception be compared across different regions fairly.
If a pair across a category boundary is easier to distinguish than an equally separated pair within a category, its advantage cannot be explained simply by a larger programmed acoustic difference.

speech1.title: The noncategorical prediction for labeling
paragraphs: A simple noncategorical observer is increasingly uncertain as a stimulus moves away from a category's best example. Its labels change gradually with distance through the continuum.
The middle /d/ region rises and falls because there are categories on either side. Such a peaked labeling curve can arise merely because the task requires choosing among a small set of responses.
Labeling by itself therefore does not settle how finely the sounds are perceived. A second task must ask whether equal acoustic differences remain equally noticeable throughout the continuum.

speech1.title: The noncategorical prediction for discrimination
paragraphs: In a **discrimination** task, listeners report whether two sounds are the same or different. Pairs can be selected with a constant step separation throughout the continuum.

If perception preserves the same sensitivity everywhere, discrimination should stay roughly constant across equally separated pairs. Labeling may vary, but crossing a label boundary should not create a special perceptual advantage.
This prediction links the two tasks: categorical perception instead predicts better discrimination where the labels switch, with worse discrimination inside a category.

speech1.title: Liberman: labeling boundaries and discrimination peaks
paragraphs: The labeling functions change sharply between /b/, /d/, and /g/. The discrimination functions peak near those changes rather than staying flat across the acoustic continuum.

A within-category pair can sound similar even when its physical separation equals that of a boundary-crossing pair. Increasing the step separation raises discriminability overall, but the boundary pattern remains important.

This combination defines the classic evidence for **categorical perception**: abrupt category assignments together with discrimination tied to those assignments. The relationship between the graphs is the key result.

speech1.title: Carrying out the categorical-perception demonstration
paragraphs: The demonstration separates two judgments. First, identify a sound along a continuum, such as beach versus peach; then judge whether two selected sounds differ.
A label boundary is located where identification changes. A discrimination comparison asks whether pairs near that location are easier to distinguish than equally separated pairs farther from it.
The two responses answer different questions. A listener can repeatedly choose one word while still showing some sensitivity to acoustic differences among tokens given that word label.

speech1.title: Comparing class identification and discrimination curves
paragraphs: The identification panels show how word choices vary across the continuum. The paired discrimination panels show responses to equally separated stimulus pairs.

Find the steep portion of each person's identification curve, then compare it with the location of that person's discrimination peak. The relevant match is between a boundary and improved discrimination.
Individual curves need not align at exactly the same stimulus number. Averaging listeners with different boundaries can soften a pattern that is sharper within a person.

speech1.title: Individual boundaries and the class task
paragraphs: Different listeners can place the boundary at different points. Despite that variation, discrimination is generally strongest for sounds assigned to different categories.
In the abbreviated class task, discrimination included only physically different pairs. Reporting different was therefore correct on every trial, even when a listener could not hear the difference.

This detail explains why the graph is a measure of detected difference under this particular design. It also distinguishes the class exercise from a full task containing both same and different trials.

speech1.title: Why class data can look noisy
paragraphs: Bear–pear and beach–peach need not produce identical curves. A listener may use the stimuli differently, and short experiments produce variable estimates from relatively few trials.

Mixing same and different trials would make response tendencies easier to assess. Repeating enough pairs and examining each person's labeling boundary would also clarify the relationship between the tasks.
The experimental question remains specific: after matching physical distance, does a pair's position relative to the listener's category boundary predict its discriminability?

speech1.title: Why reduced sensitivity can help recognition
paragraphs: Many acoustic differences do not change a word's identity. Treating every small change as a new linguistic unit would make ordinary variation across repetitions or speakers difficult to handle.

A category groups different tokens together so that later processes can access a stable phoneme or word representation. At a boundary, sensitivity is useful because the difference may distinguish words.

The advantage is selective stability: similar treatment within a category and greater differentiation between categories. This explains why being worse at some physical discriminations can accompany successful language recognition.

speech1.title: Linking categorical perception to word knowledge
paragraphs: Ganong's work asks whether known words affect the identity assigned to an ambiguous speech sound. The later speech-perception material examines this lexical influence and models that implement it.

McClelland and colleagues motivate an interactive account in which information can flow between representational levels. The assigned readings connect phoneme categorization to the larger word-recognition system.

speech1.title: Measuring infant speech discrimination
paragraphs: Infants cannot press a labeled response button, so researchers use changes in behavior. A **conditioned head turn** rewards turning when a sound changes; **high-amplitude sucking** measures sucking responses linked to sound presentation.
Repeated exposure usually reduces responding. If a new sound restores responding, the infant has detected a change rather than simply continued hearing an indistinguishable repetition.
These methods test discrimination before the infant can name a phoneme. The displayed sucking photograph illustrates the method; it is not itself the Eimas experimental result.

speech1.title: Eimas: categorical discrimination before words
paragraphs: Eimas and colleagues repeatedly presented speech sounds to infants and measured sucking. After responding declined, the sound either stayed the same or shifted within or between adult-defined categories.
A boundary-crossing change produced renewed sucking more clearly than an equally sized within-category change. The response follows perceived category structure rather than physical distance alone.
Infants therefore show categorical-like discrimination before fluent speech production. Early appearance made the phenomenon important to theories of how language abilities develop.

speech1.title: Perceptual narrowing across infancy
paragraphs: Young English-learning infants discriminate some non-English speech contrasts. With development, discrimination of those contrasts declines if they are not maintained by the language environment.
The comparison with listeners who hear the contrasts in their language ties the change to experience. The infant system becomes better aligned with distinctions useful in its surroundings.

**Perceptual narrowing** is a developmental change in which contrasts remain salient. It is not the claim that infants stop hearing sound or that all possible contrasts were equally detectable initially.

speech1.title: The initially broad perception account
paragraphs: The proposed narrative begins with broad sensitivity to speech contrasts, followed by tuning to the native language. Learning selects which distinctions continue to organize perception.
In this account, categorical speech perception is treated as an early, specialized foundation. The environment narrows an initially broad inventory rather than building every contrast from scratch.

This explanation combines an early capacity with experience-dependent change. Its claims about specialization and universality can be tested separately using nonspeech sounds, other animals, and difficult infant contrasts.

speech1.title: Separating early appearance from language specificity
paragraphs: Categorical perception occurs for nonspeech sounds and in nonhuman animals. Its appearance therefore does not automatically identify a mechanism unique to human language.
Final category decisions can also depend on the response task. A sharply divided label curve need not mean all earlier acoustic processing has become all-or-none.
Infant perception is likewise not uniform across every contrast. Some distinctions need experience to become detectable, adding category formation to the story of developmental tuning.

speech1.title: Cutting and Rosner: categories for nonspeech
paragraphs: Listeners heard sounds varying along an acoustic continuum associated with plucked and bowed qualities. They labeled the sounds and discriminated pairs at matched physical separations.
Labels changed near a boundary, and discrimination was better for pairs crossing that boundary. Sounds on the same side were harder to tell apart despite comparable physical differences.
The same labeling–discrimination relationship can therefore arise without phonemes. Categorical perception describes a perceptual organization that extends beyond speech.

speech1.title: Jusczyk: infant categories for nonspeech
paragraphs: Infants heard repeated nonspeech sounds while sucking was measured. After habituation, the sound stayed unchanged, changed within a category, or crossed a category boundary.

Sucking recovered for the between-category shift more than for a within-category shift or unchanged sound. The infant detected the acoustically different sound when it crossed the perceptual boundary.
Early categorical discrimination therefore extends beyond speech too. Infancy and categorical behavior together do not establish that the underlying capacity is language-specific.

speech1.title: Chinchillas categorize speech continua
paragraphs: Chinchillas were trained with endpoints of a voice-onset-time continuum, using a response associated with food. An **SD**, or discriminative stimulus, signals when the trained response will be rewarded.
Tests with intermediate speech sounds produced category-like changes in responding. The human comparison also shows a sharp change across the continuum.
A nonhuman auditory system can therefore organize these speech stimuli categorically. This challenges the claim that the phenomenon requires possession of human language.

speech1.title: Some infant contrasts must become salient
paragraphs: The nasal contrast /ma/–/na/ is easier for young infants than /na/–/ŋa/. These sounds differ in place of articulation, or where the constriction is made.
Narayan and colleagues found that the difficult contrast becomes more discriminable with relevant language experience. Filipino-learning infants improve across the ages shown.
Development can increase sensitivity as well as reduce it. Learning is therefore more than eliminating unused contrasts from a completely universal starting set.

speech2.title: Spoken words and the lexical–phonetic interface
paragraphs: Spoken-word recognition connects changing acoustic features, phonemes, and stored words. The **lexical–phonetic interface** is the interaction between speech-sound processing and word knowledge.
The main distinctions are when partial information moves forward and whether word-level information feeds back. Cascading and feedback answer these different questions.

speech2.title: A staged speech-perception model
paragraphs: The model passes the waveform through auditory processing, acoustic-property detection, phonetic features, segmental analysis, and lexical search. Each level expresses the signal in a different representational form.
A simple staged interpretation has phoneme identification finish before words can be recognized. Some acoustic detail can be lost as the system converts continuous variation into discrete units.
**Cascaded processing** instead permits partial activation to reach later levels. **Feedback** permits later levels to influence earlier ones; neither term merely means that processing is fast.

speech2.title: The beach–peach voicing continuum
paragraphs: Beach and peach differ at the initial stop consonant. Changing **voice onset time**, the delay between release and voicing, creates intermediate sounds along a /b/–/p/ continuum.
Identification changes from one word to the other, while discrimination is strongest around the boundary. These final judgments reproduce the familiar categorical pattern.
The next question concerns what happens before the final choice. Sounds receiving the same word label might still activate competing words by different amounts.

speech2.title: Thresholded transmission
paragraphs: In a **threshold model**, information is passed to the next level only when activation crosses a required level. The phoneme decision acts like a gate on what reaches word recognition.

Graded feature evidence can therefore be converted into a more discrete phoneme signal. Once the gate selects /b/, later processing would receive that category rather than the remaining within-category uncertainty.
This makes a prediction about word competition: acoustic differences that do not change the phoneme output should not continuously change activation of its lexical competitor.

speech2.title: Cascaded transmission
paragraphs: In a **cascaded model**, activation flows forward while the earlier level is still changing. A phoneme need not be fully settled before it begins activating words.
A sound closer to the /b/–/p/ boundary can activate more /p/-consistent competitors even when the final response remains /b/. The graded feature input continues to matter downstream.
A step-like final label can coexist with this process. Categorization at the response stage does not require every internal representation to switch categorically at the same moment.

speech2.title: The lumber-mill analogy
paragraphs: The lumber mill takes trees and produces lumber; the factory takes lumber and produces a furniture kit; the customer assembles that kit. Each stage requires the previous stage's transformed output.
A factory cannot assemble a shipment that has not arrived. Similarly, a strongly staged language model waits for the required earlier representation before beginning the next operation.
The analogy captures dependence on completed inputs. It explains what thresholded transmission would mean for the timing of phoneme and word recognition.

speech2.title: Waiting for a completed representation
paragraphs: The important feature of the furniture chain is its input requirement. A later layer accepts a particular finished representation, not every partial state of the preceding layer.
Translated to speech, lexical processing would wait for phoneme-level output. Unresolved acoustic uncertainty would be handled upstream before lexical search begins.
Testing this account requires a measure during recognition. A final mouse click alone could hide uncertainty that was active earlier.

speech2.title: The food-web analogy
paragraphs: In a **food web**, a change in one population affects others through ongoing connections. A drought alters plants, which influences consumers and then predators while the system continues operating.
Cascaded processing has the same continuous character: partially changed activation at one level changes the input to other levels immediately rather than after a finished package is delivered.
Feedback adds influence in the reverse direction. The analogy separates continuous forward propagation from the additional possibility of reciprocal interactions.

speech2.title: Testing thresholds against cascades
paragraphs: Both accounts can produce a final bear or pear response. The decisive comparison asks whether fine acoustic changes within one response category affect competition before that response.
A visual-world task records looks to pictures while a spoken target unfolds. Looking toward the alternative picture provides a time-sensitive index of its involvement in recognition.
If competitor looks grow gradually near the category boundary, information has affected lexical processing without having to change the final category decision.

speech2.title: McMurray: the visual-world method
paragraphs: Participants viewed pictures including a /b/–/p/ competitor pair and heard a token from a voice-onset-time continuum. Eye tracking measured where they looked as they identified it.
The pictures make possible word interpretations visible. Bear can be the selected target while pear briefly attracts attention as a competing interpretation.
Varying the acoustic token while preserving the picture set tests whether distance from the phoneme boundary changes ongoing lexical competition.

speech2.title: A categorical final choice
paragraphs: Participants clicked the picture matching the spoken token. The identification curve was step-like: one part of the continuum generally led to bear, the other to pear.
This reproduces categorical responding in an ordinary recognition task. It does not yet reveal whether all bear responses were equally certain at every earlier moment.
Eye movements supply the missing time course. They allow comparison of tokens that end in the same click but differ in the strength of the alternative they briefly activate.

speech2.title: Competitor looks reveal graded ambiguity
paragraphs: Tokens nearer the phoneme boundary produced more looks to the competing picture. The final click could remain the same while the moment-by-moment distribution of looks changed.
The result means that within-category acoustic differences reached word-level processing. A less prototypical bear token created greater temporary competition from pear.
Recognition is therefore richer than the final categorical label. The eye trace reveals partial activation that a single endpoint response conceals.

speech2.title: Aligning looks with the category boundary
paragraphs: The reorganized graph expresses competitor looking relative to distance from the category boundary. Competitor activity increases as the input approaches that boundary.
This comparison focuses on **category goodness**: some members fit a category more clearly than others. They can share a final label while differing in how strongly the alternative remains active.
The gradual relationship fits continuous propagation. It is harder to explain by a phoneme gate that sends an identical, fully resolved symbol for every token inside one category.

speech2.title: How a cascade produces the eye-movement result
paragraphs: A bilabial stop can activate features consistent with both /b/ and /p/ by different amounts. **Bilabial** means produced with the two lips; voicing helps distinguish the competing consonants.
Graded feature activation influences phoneme activation and then candidate words. A near-boundary token leaves more activity in the competitor than a clearly voiced token does.
The resulting looks track this competition before a decision. The same final word can emerge from different amounts of earlier uncertainty.

speech2.title: Andruski: partial input can activate meaning
paragraphs: Nonwords resembling real words can facilitate related meanings: beace primes war, and ging primes queen. **Semantic priming** means a preceding item facilitates processing of a meaning-related target.
A near-word input can partially activate peace or king without being a correct spoken instance of that word. Their meanings can then influence the following target.

Partial acoustic evidence can therefore have consequences as far as the lexical and semantic levels. Recognition does not need a perfectly completed phoneme sequence before any downstream activation occurs.

speech2.title: Why the threshold-only account struggles
paragraphs: A threshold that passes only the chosen phoneme loses the differences among tokens assigned to that phoneme. It would give later levels essentially the same category output for those tokens.
McMurray's competitor looks vary gradually even among tokens receiving the same final label. The variation therefore survives into recognition instead of vanishing at a discrete gate.
Cascading explains how this can happen: partial activation is continuously transmitted. The evidence concerns the flow of uncertainty, not the disappearance of phoneme categories.

speech2.title: Adding lexical feedback
paragraphs: The model includes connections from words back to phonemes. A partially active word can reinforce the phoneme sequence consistent with that word.
**Feedback** differs from cascading: cascading describes continuous forward flow; feedback describes information traveling from a later representational level toward an earlier one.
The two can work together. Acoustic input starts several candidates, and lexical knowledge can then change the balance among their component speech sounds.

speech2.title: Ganong: real words bias phoneme labels
paragraphs: Ganong constructed continua between a real word and a nonword, such as corpse and gorpse. The initial sound was varied in small voice-onset-time steps.
An ambiguous consonant could be interpreted in a way that produces a known word. A different surrounding sequence could favor the other consonant instead.
Comparing the labeling functions tests a **lexical effect** on phoneme identification. The crucial stimuli are ambiguous enough that word knowledge can affect their interpretation.

speech2.title: The late-correction prediction
paragraphs: A late-correction account leaves the initial phoneme percept unchanged, then biases a report toward a real word. Word knowledge acts after an otherwise ordinary categorical decision.
This predicts a response adjustment rather than a relocation of the phoneme boundary itself. Its shape can be contrasted with the boundary-shift prediction in the next comparison.
The experiment therefore asks more than whether words are favored overall. Where the two labeling curves differ across the continuum helps distinguish the accounts.

speech2.title: The boundary-shift prediction
paragraphs: If word knowledge changes the category boundary, its largest effect should occur for ambiguous sounds near that boundary. Clear endpoint tokens need little lexical help.
The same intermediate acoustic input can receive different labels when one surrounding sequence makes /k/ a word and another makes /g/ a word. The transition point shifts with lexical context.
This is a selective interaction between evidence and knowledge. It does not predict that every clearly heard consonant should be overwritten whenever a word is available.

speech2.title: Ganong's observed labeling curves
paragraphs: The observed curves resemble a change around the category boundary more than a uniform late correction. Lexical context has its greatest influence where the consonant is uncertain.
Known words therefore affect how the ambiguous speech sequence is categorized. The shape of the effect is part of the evidence, rather than only the total number of word responses.
Later interactive models implement this with lexical-to-phoneme feedback: activated words strengthen the speech sounds that support them.

speech2.title: TRACE: activation changes as speech unfolds
paragraphs: **TRACE** represents interacting features, phonemes, and words over time. An unfolding input activates several words compatible with its early sounds.
The plots show candidates changing activation rather than appearing only after the entire word is heard. Later input changes how well each candidate fits.
A simulation connects a proposed mechanism to a time course. Its changing word and phoneme activity provides a process-level account of lexical effects on an ambiguous initial consonant.

speech2.title: Why the final /g/ favors plug
paragraphs: Early input can partially support plug, blood, or blush. When the final /g/ arrives, it strongly favors plug over the competitors whose endings do not match.
Increasing plug activation feeds back to its phonemes. This can strengthen the interpretation of the initial sound that makes the full input a word.
The sequence illustrates interaction across time and levels: later evidence changes word competition, and the winning lexical candidate influences an earlier speech-sound interpretation.

speech2.title: TRACE and interactive activation
paragraphs: TRACE shares principles with the **interactive activation** approach to written-word recognition. Representational levels activate compatible candidates, while competition helps select among alternatives.
Speech adds an important temporal demand. A spoken word arrives progressively, so candidates must be updated as successive sounds become available.

The relationship is mechanistic rather than merely visual: reciprocal activation and competitive selection can explain word recognition in different input modalities while respecting their different time courses.

speech2.title: Categories coexist with interaction
paragraphs: Equal physical differences can remain easier to hear across category boundaries. Neither cascading nor lexical feedback requires that this basic categorical-perception result disappear.
What changes is the claim that a word-recognition system waits passively for finished phonemes. Acoustic uncertainty can affect words, and word knowledge can affect ambiguous phonemes.
The **lexical–phonetic interface** is therefore interactive. Stable final categories can emerge from a process that retains graded information and exchanges influence between levels.

speech2.title: From words to sentence ambiguity
paragraphs: The sentence-processing reading extends the ambiguity question to larger structures. Words can fit more than one grammatical arrangement while a sentence unfolds.

The relevant connection is timing: does one process finish before another begins, or do several sources of information constrain interpretation together? This prepares the move from phoneme and word competition to competing sentence analyses.

speech2.title: The cohort effect in spoken-word recognition
paragraphs: As a spoken word begins, words sharing its onset form a **cohort** of candidates. Listeners can look toward both the target and an onset-sharing competitor before the ending separates them.
In the visual-world display, the target gains looks as evidence accumulates. The cohort competitor attracts early looks, then loses support when the rest of the sound no longer matches.
The eye-movement time course shows recognition operating during the word. The system need not wait for a completed acoustic word before considering lexical candidates.

speech2.title: Why the time course matters
paragraphs: The simulation and eye traces track changing activity for targets and different competitors. Their peaks and declines reveal when a candidate is temporarily plausible.
A final correct click compresses that history into one answer. Time-resolved measures preserve the competition that occurred on the way to the answer.
This links cohort effects to graded category goodness: both show information influencing recognition before a final categorical response is issued.

aphasias.title: Aphasia: language after brain injury
paragraphs: **Aphasia** is an acquired disruption of language associated with brain injury. Different patterns of speaking and understanding can reveal which operations a language task requires.
The central comparison is between a loss of linguistic knowledge and difficulty using that knowledge under processing demands. Carefully designed comprehension tasks help separate these explanations.

aphasias.title: Centers, connections, and disconnections
paragraphs: Early neurologists such as Wernicke and Lichtheim described specialized centers joined by pathways. Damage to a connection could disrupt one operation while leaving other operations available.

In the diagram, comprehension and verbatim repetition can fail through different disconnections. **Repetition** means reproducing what was heard, which need not be identical to understanding its meaning.
A box-and-arrow model states which representations communicate. This makes distinct predicted impairment patterns possible instead of treating every language difficulty as the same disorder.

aphasias.title: The Geschwind–Wernicke framework
paragraphs: Geschwind revived a connected-system account of brain and language. The diagram places auditory, motor, and connecting regions within an anatomical model.
By this period, linguistics also distinguished computations such as syntax from lexical knowledge. Clinical differences could therefore be interpreted using more specific candidate functions.
A **double dissociation** compares contrasting patterns of impairment. It can motivate separating operations, but the task definitions determine which operations the comparison actually tests.

aphasias.title: Fluency, agrammatism, and comprehension
paragraphs: Broca-type speech often contains word-finding pauses, omitted grammatical morphemes, and disturbed word order. **Agrammatism** refers to this reduced or disrupted grammatical organization.

Wernicke-type speech can be fluent and well articulated while containing substitutions, invented words, and comprehension problems. Fluency describes the flow of speech rather than whether its content is accurate.
Everyday conversation may make comprehension seem better than controlled testing shows. The passage also distinguishes behavioral syndromes from a perfectly one-to-one match with a named brain area.

aphasias.title: Telegraphic speech versus fluent word salad
paragraphs: **Telegraphic speech** retains important content words but has difficulty with grammatical particles, inflections, and ordering. The listener may infer an intended message from the surviving words.
Wernicke-type **word salad** can preserve the outward rhythm and rough syntax of speech while word selection and meaningful organization break down. A **neologism** is an invented word form.
These profiles suggest a contrast between grammatical organization and lexical selection. The contrast motivates experiments rather than replacing the need to test those functions directly.

aphasias.title: Broca's original cases and apraxia of speech
paragraphs: Broca's original patients had profound problems producing articulate speech. This historical description is not identical to the later syndrome defined mainly through agrammatic language.
**Apraxia of speech** concerns planning or controlling speech movements. A person may have difficulty producing the movements without having lost all grammatical knowledge.
Calling both patterns Broca-related can hide this distinction. The question is whether the observed failure belongs to motor execution, linguistic structure, or a combination.

aphasias.title: Why grammar and the lexicon were separated
paragraphs: The **lexicon** contains word-level representations; **grammar** organizes combinations and structural relations. The proposed aphasia dichotomy maps Wernicke-type problems onto lexical activation and Broca-type problems onto grammar.
Formal linguistic arguments made this separation plausible by distinguishing grammatical structure from meaning. A sentence can be syntactically organized even when its meaning is strange.
The clinical prediction is specific: a grammar impairment should affect tasks that need structural relationships, including comprehension when word meaning alone cannot supply the answer.

aphasias.title: Functional and positional levels in production
paragraphs: The production framework separates selecting lexical items from organizing their grammatical positions and forms. **Lemmas** are lexical representations linked to intended meanings; positional processes arrange grammatical structure.
The relationship between a word and its referent is often arbitrary. Affixes and structural combinations instead reflect rules governing how pieces are assembled.

The error easy enoughly illustrates morphology participating in production processes rather than being only a stored whole-word meaning. This is why the grammar–lexicon contrast involves more than long words versus short words.

aphasias.title: Testing grammar during comprehension
paragraphs: A listener can seem to understand a sentence by combining familiar meanings and contextual expectations. This success does not necessarily show that every syntactic dependency was computed.
An autonomous-parser account proposes structural computations that can be distinguished from meaning. To test them, sentence materials must make structure determine the intended interpretation.
Broca-type patients could therefore follow many conversations while struggling with sentences whose grammatical relationships cannot be recovered from familiar event knowledge.

aphasias.title: From articulation to a syntactic hypothesis
paragraphs: Broca's historical observation separated articulate speech from comprehension. A later theory asks a different question: can grammatical processing be impaired across speaking and understanding?

A comprehension task reduces the need to produce speech. If difficulty remains when the participant can simply choose a picture, impaired articulation alone is insufficient to explain that response pattern.
The best materials isolate who performs an action and who receives it. They force structural information to contribute instead of letting the task be solved entirely through familiar meanings.

aphasias.title: Competence and performance
paragraphs: **Competence** refers to linguistic knowledge; **performance** is its use under actual processing and response demands. Motor difficulties can change speech output even if some underlying knowledge remains.

Jackson's point is that the behavior observed after injury is what the person can still accomplish. A short, agrammatic utterance may reflect an adaptation to difficulty rather than a literal picture of an erased grammar.
Caramazza and Zurif therefore examined comprehension. The aim was to see whether grammatical relationships cause difficulty when the required response does not depend on producing a fluent sentence.

aphasias.title: Why man bites dog is informative
paragraphs: For the dog bit the man, word meanings and familiar event knowledge favor the same interpretation as ordinary English word order. Several routes can lead to a correct response.
In the dog that the man is biting is angry, the man performs the biting and the dog receives it. A dog-bites-man expectation gives the wrong answer.

This sentence separates **semantic heuristics**, shortcuts based on likely events, from computing the actual relationship. Choosing the matching picture requires tracking the embedded grammatical structure.

aphasias.title: Caramazza and Zurif's sentence contrasts
paragraphs: Control sentences provide relatively straightforward action descriptions. Other conditions embed one clause inside another, increasing the need to connect the nouns to their grammatical roles.

**Semantically constrained** items, such as an apple being eaten by a boy, can be supported by plausibility. **Reversible** items contain participants that could exchange roles, while improbable items make the intended relation conflict with common expectations.

Comparing these conditions asks when plausibility can compensate for structural difficulty. The task is not merely recognizing nouns; it is selecting the picture showing the specified action relation.

aphasias.title: The sentence–picture matching results
paragraphs: Healthy controls performed well across sentence types. Wernicke-type patients were poor more broadly, consistent with substantial comprehension difficulty.

Broca-type patients had particular difficulty when structure conflicted with likely roles or when the nouns could plausibly exchange roles. The trouble concerned keeping who did what to whom straight.

This pattern supported the proposal that syntax contributes a distinct operation. It showed why everyday comprehension can conceal problems that become visible in carefully contrasted sentence materials.

aphasias.title: Defining the operation more precisely
paragraphs: Broad descriptions such as fluent or poor comprehension summarize behavior but combine many processes. A language theory can suggest finer distinctions, such as lexical access versus structural role assignment.
Experiments then make the proposed distinction observable. Sentence–picture matching separates recognizing content words from using the grammar to connect their referents.

The resulting structure–function question concerns particular operations rather than a whole faculty called language. The explanatory value comes from linking a defined task contrast to a defined impairment pattern.

aphasias.title: Dick: four ways to describe the same action
paragraphs: Participants indicated which animal performed the action. In the dog is biting the cat, the dog is the agent; it remains the agent in it's the cat that the dog is biting.
The four forms were active, subject cleft, object cleft, and passive. **Object clefts** and **passives** require interpreting a first-mentioned noun that is not simply the acting participant.
Holding the event relation constant while varying its expression tests sensitivity to sentence form. The target is the agent, not whichever animal happens to be named first.

aphasias.title: Patient performance across sentence forms
paragraphs: Broca-type patients struggled particularly with object clefts and passives relative to easier forms. The pattern resembles the earlier difficulty with noncanonical or structurally demanding relationships.
The participant must map the sentence onto the correct actor while resisting a first-noun-as-agent shortcut. That shortcut works for many active sentences but fails for an object cleft.
The graph compares performance patterns across groups rather than diagnosing grammar from one missed item. Both overall accuracy and the additional cost of particular forms matter.

aphasias.title: Healthy listeners under processing stress
paragraphs: Healthy undergraduates also became especially vulnerable on object clefts and passives when speech was accelerated or a secondary memory task added demands.
The manipulation changes available processing resources rather than giving the participants a brain lesion. The resulting selective difficulty resembles part of the patient pattern.
A structurally selective deficit can therefore emerge through **performance** demands. The shared pattern raises the possibility that demanding sentences expose a more general processing bottleneck.

aphasias.title: Saygin: actions without words
paragraphs: Patients matched an action to an object using linguistic and nonlinguistic stimuli. The drawings make meaningful relations available without requiring a sentence to carry all the information.
Broca-type patients had difficulty in both versions. Removing language did not eliminate the relevant task difficulty.

The result connects linguistic action interpretation with broader action or event processing. It tests whether the impairment is confined to sentence grammar by preserving the relation while changing its presentation.

aphasias.title: Relating action matching to lesion location
paragraphs: Performance on the nonverbal task was associated with damage involving Broca's area. The anatomical relationship therefore extended beyond a language-only version of the task.
A **lesion–behavior association** relates the location of damaged tissue to measured performance. Here the behavior involves interpreting or matching an action relation without a spoken sentence.
The evidence motivates a functional description broader than grammar alone. A region can contribute to language tasks because those tasks also depend on operations used outside language.

aphasias.title: Environmental sounds and Wernicke-type deficits
paragraphs: Patients matched environmental sounds to pictures and also completed a verbal version. An environmental sound conveys information about an event or object without being a word.
Wernicke-type patients were particularly poor, and the reported verbal–nonverbal difference was not significant. Their difficulty extended to extracting meaning from sounds outside speech.
The comparison preserves auditory meaning matching while changing whether the input is linguistic. This helps explain why poor spoken comprehension need not identify a language-exclusive deficit.

aphasias.title: Auditory meaning and posterior damage
paragraphs: The lesion maps relate poor sound–picture matching to damage involving Wernicke's area. Associations are shown for both verbal and nonverbal inputs.
The overlap matters because both tasks require connecting an auditory pattern with an appropriate meaning. One uses words; the other uses meaningful environmental sounds.

The anatomical result therefore fits a contribution to auditory comprehension broader than word labels alone. Behavioral task comparisons and lesion maps address the same functional question from different directions.

aphasias.title: What the competing aphasia accounts explain
paragraphs: A grammar–lexicon account predicts dissociable linguistic operations. A broader processing account asks whether similar difficulties occur when comparable demands are imposed without language.

Controlled sentences, action matching, and environmental-sound matching give these proposals measurable predictions. Accuracy patterns are compared across conditions and related quantitatively to lesions.
The resulting debate concerns what a region or impairment contributes to a task. Naming a syndrome is the starting point for explaining the behavior, not the entire explanation.

aphasias.title: Connecting aphasia to development
paragraphs: The next topic asks how language functions emerge rather than how they change after injury. Developmental evidence can help identify the contributions of experience and initial learning capacities.
The connection is functional: successful language depends on several interacting operations. Their appearance, change, and vulnerability can be studied through carefully chosen behavioral tasks.

aphasias.title: Voxel-based lesion–symptom mapping
paragraphs: **Voxel-based lesion–symptom mapping** compares damage at small brain locations with differences in behavior across many patients. A voxel is a small three-dimensional unit in a brain image.

The displayed maps associate broad fluency deficits more with anterior regions and broad comprehension deficits more with posterior regions. This supports a rough production–perception separation at that level of description.
The particular symptom measure determines the interpretation. Broad fluency maps and precise action-matching contrasts ask related but differently detailed questions about brain function.

development1.title: How speech perception develops
paragraphs: Language development asks how an infant's changing abilities arise from initial capacities and experience. Speech perception is especially useful because it can be measured before fluent speaking.
The lecture moves from categorical perception to learning from sound distributions and social interaction. The common question is what experience changes in the perceptual system.

development1.title: Nativist explanations of language acquisition
paragraphs: **Generativity** is the ability to produce and understand new sentences. Chomsky argued that acquiring a language involves identifying an abstract grammar rather than memorizing a list of utterances.

The critique of simple behaviorism has two parts: grammatical similarity is not reducible to straightforward surface resemblance, and children are not consistently rewarded for grammar and punished for ungrammaticality.

A **nativist** account proposes innate knowledge about possible languages, called Universal Grammar, together with language-specific acquisition processes. Speed and broadly comparable grammatical outcomes motivated this proposal.

development1.title: Why categorical perception seemed specialized
paragraphs: Categorical perception makes equal physical differences unequal perceptually. Sounds crossing a phoneme boundary are distinguished more easily than sounds within one category.
Early theories interpreted this as an auditory signal being translated into language-relevant symbols. Its apparent restriction to humans and speech made a specialized mechanism seem plausible.
The key distinction is between describing the perceptual pattern and explaining its origin. Similarity defined by a category can emerge through different kinds of learning or initial organization.

development1.title: Infant methods: head turns and sucking
paragraphs: A conditioned head turn rewards an infant for turning when a sound changes. High-amplitude sucking instead measures sucking linked to presentation of the auditory stimulus.
Repetition causes **habituation**, a decline in response. A renewed response after a sound change indicates that the infant detected a difference.
The measure supplies evidence without asking for a verbal category label. The comparison must specify whether the sound stayed the same, changed within a category, or crossed a boundary.

development1.title: Eimas: comparing equal changes in VOT
paragraphs: Infants heard repeated speech tokens varying in **voice onset time**, the interval between stop release and the onset of voicing. Sucking was measured before and after a stimulus shift.
A between-category shift produced stronger recovery than a matched within-category shift. An unchanged condition supplied a comparison for responding without a new sound.

The result is categorical-like discrimination early in life. Infants distinguished the changes according to their relation to a speech boundary, rather than responding equally to every physical shift.

development1.title: Why an early infant result mattered
paragraphs: At around four months, many motor and visual skills are still developing, and speech production is only beginning to resemble vowel-like sounds. Categorical discrimination appears early relative to those milestones.
If the ability were unique to speech and humans, its early emergence would fit an account of an innate language specialization. This made the Eimas finding influential.
Early presence establishes when a behavior can be observed. The claims that it is language-specific or independent of learning require additional comparisons, which the following experiments provide.

development1.title: Werker: perceptual narrowing
paragraphs: Young English-learning infants detect contrasts that distinguish sounds in Hindi or Salish even though those contrasts are not used in English. Older English-learning infants show reduced discrimination.
Infants remain sensitive to distinctions supported by their own linguistic environment. Experience changes which differences organize perception most effectively.
**Perceptual narrowing** describes this increasing tuning. The loss concerns particular distinctions; it is not a general decline in hearing or the ability to learn any new information.

development1.title: The citizens-of-the-world narrative
paragraphs: The proposed account starts with many available phonetic contrasts. Exposure to the native language selects a smaller set that remains useful for distinguishing its words.
Learning is therefore described as choosing among innately available categories. A broad initial capacity becomes specialized through the child's environment.

This narrative makes concrete predictions: categorical perception should be special to language, and infants should begin with access to the relevant contrasts. Both claims can be tested independently.

development1.title: What a fuller developmental account must explain
paragraphs: Categorical patterns also occur with nonspeech sounds, nonhuman listeners, and different task demands. The same outward behavior does not always identify a uniquely linguistic mechanism.
Infant contrasts differ in initial salience, meaning how easy they are to detect. Some improve with relevant experience instead of being present early and then lost.
A developmental explanation therefore needs both category tuning and category formation. It must explain why experience can strengthen some distinctions while reducing sensitivity to others.

development1.title: Cutting and Rosner's nonspeech continuum
paragraphs: Adults labeled nonspeech sounds with plucked or bowed qualities and discriminated equally separated pairs. The sounds varied in an acoustic property such as their onset characteristics.
Labeling changed around a category boundary, and discrimination was best near that boundary. The physically matched within-category changes were less noticeable.
Categorical perception can therefore organize nonspeech input. Its signature is the relationship between category labeling and discrimination, not simply the presence of spoken syllables.

development1.title: Jusczyk: infant nonspeech categories
paragraphs: Infants first heard a repeated nonspeech sound until sucking declined. The stimulus then remained unchanged, shifted within a category, or crossed a boundary.
Renewed sucking appeared most clearly for the between-category condition. The within-category condition resembled the unchanged condition more closely despite a physical change.
Infants can therefore show the categorical pattern outside speech. The result connects early auditory organization with a broader perceptual capacity.

development1.title: Chinchilla speech categorization
paragraphs: Chinchillas learned to respond to endpoint speech stimuli when that response was rewarded with food. The trained **SD** signaled that a response would have its rewarded consequence.
Intermediate voice-onset times were then used to trace the response curve. The change between endpoint-consistent responses was category-like, comparable in broad form to human labeling.
Possessing human language is not required for this organization of speech sounds. The experiment separates an animal's auditory categorization from the specifically human uses made of phonemes.

development1.title: Narayan: not every contrast starts equally clear
paragraphs: Young infants detected /ma/–/na/ more readily than /na/–/ŋa/. The latter distinguishes two nasal places of articulation at the beginning of a syllable.
Looking behavior changed when an easy contrast switched, but not comparably for the difficult contrast. The same method therefore reveals unequal sensitivity to different speech distinctions.
The initial state is not a universal inventory in which every possible contrast is equally available. Acoustic salience is part of what the learning system begins with.

development1.title: Experience can create a stronger distinction
paragraphs: Filipino-learning infants improved on /na/–/ŋa/ between the younger and older ages shown. Their environment provides information that makes this contrast linguistically relevant.
Older infants showed a clearer behavioral difference between same and change trials. The ability grows with experience instead of merely surviving from an equally sensitive initial state.
Learning can therefore add effective distinctions. This complements perceptual narrowing: development changes the organization of perception in both directions.

development1.title: Emergentist learning and associations
paragraphs: An **emergentist** account explains organized behavior through learning mechanisms sensitive to regularities in experience. An association strengthens when events reliably occur together.
In the neuron illustration, food already activates a salivation response. Repeated pairing allows the bell-related connection to become stronger, so the bell can help activate that response.
Speech learning requires extending this principle to pattern recognition. The relevant input is not merely a reward but the distribution and co-occurrence of acoustic properties across many sounds.

development1.title: Learning a vowel distribution
paragraphs: The vowel-space plot places productions using F1 and F2. A vowel category forms a cloud because no speaker produces exactly the same resonance pattern every time.
A statistical learner can track where observations cluster. A **prototype**, a particularly representative example, could correspond to the distribution's mean or most frequent region.
This turns category learning into discovering structure in variable input. Overlapping clouds explain why a single formant pair may remain ambiguous even after useful categories have formed.

development1.title: Maye: one peak versus two peaks
paragraphs: Infants passively heard a continuum distributed around either one peak or two. **Unimodal** exposure emphasizes one central cluster; **bimodal** exposure emphasizes two clusters.
Test trials alternated tokens 3 and 6 or repeated a token. Those critical tokens occurred equally often during exposure, so their individual familiarity does not explain the group contrast.

Only the bimodal group showed clear sensitivity to the alternating versus nonalternating test. The distribution changed whether the same two sounds were treated as distinct, supporting learning from statistical structure.

development1.title: Learning through social interaction
paragraphs: Infants exposed to live, interactive Mandarin showed phonetic learning more clearly than groups receiving television or audio exposure. The contrast concerns the context of language experience, not simply the presence of sound.

In another study, mothers' responses either followed their infant's vocalizations or occurred on a noncontingent schedule. **Contingent** feedback depends on the infant's own action; it increased the quantity and complexity of vocalizations.

Social exchange can help by reinforcing behavior or directing attention to useful information. These mechanisms connect other people to the learning process rather than treating exposure as an undifferentiated count of sounds.

development1.title: Statistical learning is constrained
paragraphs: A learner must discover which properties distinguish categories. Speaker identity and speech rate vary widely but do not define the same linguistic contrasts as phonetic cues.
Earlier learning changes later learning by making some distinctions easier to preserve or acquire. This creates a connection between statistical learning and sensitive periods.

Social and interactive context also changes what is learned. A constrained statistical account therefore includes the properties attended to, the learner's existing organization, and the context in which the input arrives.

development2.title: Finding words, meanings, and constructions
paragraphs: Language development includes separating words from speech, linking them to meanings, and combining them into structures. Success at one problem does not automatically solve the next.

**Morphemes** are meaningful grammatical pieces, and **constructions** are patterns that connect forms with uses or meanings. The experiments ask what children know before their own utterances become long and fluent.

development2.title: Why speech does not supply printed spaces
paragraphs: The acoustic signal has no consistent physical boundary between every pair of words. Closures and pauses can occur within words as well as between them.
A learner therefore cannot simply split the waveform wherever silence appears. **Segmentation** means discovering word-sized units within this connected stream.
The problem is harder for a beginner who does not already know the words. Regularities within the signal must help establish the units that will later support recognition.

development2.title: Stress and phonotactic cues to boundaries
paragraphs: **Phonotactics** concerns which sound sequences occur within a language's words. An unusual sequence can suggest that a word boundary lies between its sounds.

English often stresses the first syllable of a word. Infants familiarized with kingdom recognized it in connected passages more clearly than infants familiarized with device, whose stress falls later.
Stress can therefore help locate word beginnings in English. Isolated words and phonotactic regularities supply additional cues, and different languages can assign these cues different usefulness.

development2.title: Pretty baby and transitional probability
paragraphs: A **transitional probability** is how likely one syllable is to follow another. In pretty baby, the first syllable of pretty strongly predicts its own second syllable.

The final syllable of pretty can instead be followed by many words, making one specific across-word continuation less reliable. The frequency ratios compare a pair's occurrences with the occurrences of its starting syllable.
High within-word predictability and lower across-word predictability can help locate boundaries. The learner tracks conditional relationships rather than simply counting which syllables are common.

development2.title: Why probabilities are cues, not printed boundaries
paragraphs: A syllable is often more predictable after another syllable inside a word than after a word ending. This makes a drop in predictability a useful segmentation cue.
The road ahead versus a head and ice cream versus I scream show that acoustic sequences can support multiple divisions. Context can change which division is meaningful.
Statistical segmentation is therefore probabilistic. Several sources of information can support an interpretation, and the same sound sequence need not carry one unavoidable boundary structure.

development2.title: Saffran: isolating statistical information
paragraphs: Infants heard continuously presented artificial speech made from simple consonant–vowel syllables. The stream was monotone, without boundary-defining changes in pitch, amplitude, duration, or pauses.
Repeated three-syllable units such as tokibu and gopila created strong internal relationships. Boundaries were available through the transition statistics rather than ordinary speech cues.
This design tests whether statistical structure is sufficient to affect segmentation. A successful response cannot be attributed to a pause conveniently marking each artificial word.

development2.title: The unsegmented artificial stream
paragraphs: The printed syllable stream illustrates what the infant hears without inserted word spaces. The same small set of three-syllable units recurs in different orders.

A starting syllable reliably predicts the rest of its unit, while a unit ending may lead to several possible next units. These conditional patterns are present even when the stream looks like one continuous string.
The learner's problem is to discover recurring groupings from those relationships. The experimenter knows the units, but the infant must recover them from exposure.

development2.title: Making the hidden groupings visible
paragraphs: Coloring the recurring units reveals the structure already present in the unsegmented stream. The colors are an explanatory aid; they were not an extra cue in the infant's auditory input.

Across repetitions, syllables inside a unit stay together more reliably than syllables straddling a boundary. The same sequence therefore supports different predictions at internal and boundary positions.
The comparison between the plain and colored versions separates what the input contains statistically from what it explicitly marks. Repetition can reveal structure without audible spaces.

development2.title: Words versus frequency-matched part-words
paragraphs: A **part-word** spans a trained word boundary. It can occur just as often as a real artificial word while having lower internal transitional probabilities.
In the example, GOPILA and BU-GIKO each occur twice. But GI follows BU on only some occasions, whereas the internal transitions in GOPILA are fully predictable in that sequence.
Matching frequency tests the proposed learning mechanism. If infants distinguish these sequences, mere familiarity with how often the whole string occurred is insufficient to explain the difference.

development2.title: Interpreting the novelty preference
paragraphs: Infants looked longer toward part-word test items than toward trained words. Here the longer response is a **novelty preference**, showing that the groups of syllables were treated differently.
Because part-words were matched in occurrence frequency, simple repetition count does not explain why they were less familiar in structure. The conditional syllable relationships distinguish them.
The result supports statistical segmentation. Longer looking does not always mean greater familiarity; its interpretation depends on the task and exposure design.

development2.title: Segmentation does not supply meaning
paragraphs: Finding a stable spoken form such as cat identifies a recurring unit. It does not determine which object, property, or event that form refers to.
**Reference** is the relation between an expression and what the speaker intends it to pick out. Word learning requires connecting the discovered form to an appropriate interpretation.
The next experiments therefore move from recognizing repeated sound patterns to using the social and conceptual context in which words are spoken.

development2.title: The inductive problem of word meaning
paragraphs: A speaker says cat near an animal. The sound could in principle refer to the whole animal, its fur, a body part, its movement, a category, or the individual named Felix.
The **hypothesis space** is this set of candidate interpretations. One co-occurrence between word and scene does not uniquely select the intended meaning.

Word learners need ways to narrow those possibilities. Attention, speaker intention, and default assumptions make the mapping problem more manageable than unrestricted association with everything visible.

development2.title: Joint attention and reference
paragraphs: **Joint attention** means sharing an attentional focus with another person. Gaze following begins around the age indicated in the lecture and helps a child connect communication with an attended object.
Looking where a speaker looks is useful because a word is intentionally directed toward something. The relevant scene includes the speaker's relation to the object, not only the object's presence.
Shared attention therefore supplies evidence about reference. It helps distinguish what the adult means from other things happening at the same moment.

development2.title: Baldwin: interaction versus a voice behind a screen
paragraphs: In the joint-attention condition, an adult interacting with the infant labeled the object the infant was handling. In the other condition, a voice behind a screen supplied the label.
Eighteen-month-olds learned the new word in the joint-attention condition but not in the no-joint-attention condition. Simply hearing a label while touching an object was not equally effective.
The result connects learning to a communicative interaction. Shared attention helps make the spoken form an intentional reference to the object.

development2.title: Follow-in and discrepant labeling
paragraphs: In **follow-in labeling**, the speaker looks at and names the toy already occupying the infant's attention. In **discrepant labeling**, the speaker attends to a different toy, such as one in a bucket.

The contrast separates the infant's current focus from the speaker's intended referent. A purely simultaneous-association strategy would favor the infant's own toy even when the adult names something else.

Following the speaker's gaze provides another route to the mapping. The key question is whether infants use information about another person's intention rather than only their own momentary attention.

development2.title: Using gaze as evidence about a new word
paragraphs: A gaze-direction demonstration asks which object the speaker is looking toward when giving a new label. Eye direction can distinguish an intended referent from a competing object.
The informative comparison is between the child's focus and the adult's focus. They can coincide, or the child can use the adult's gaze to redirect the interpretation.
This page marks a demonstration in the source PDF. The underlying concept is intentional reference through gaze; a still PDF does not reproduce the original moving demonstration.

development2.title: Akhtar: emotional and behavioral cues
paragraphs: A new label can occur while an adult searches among objects or reacts differently to them. Facial expression and behavior help identify what the adult intends.
Infants use those cues to select a referent for the novel word. The relevant information is not only which object was physically present when the sound occurred.
Learning therefore includes interpreting an interaction. An adult's satisfaction, attention, or goal can narrow the candidate meanings of a new expression.

development2.title: Reading intention from an interaction
paragraphs: An intentional-cues demonstration highlights that naming occurs within goal-directed behavior. The learner observes what the speaker is trying to find or communicate.
A response that identifies the intended object follows the adult's goal rather than treating every encounter as an equally good label–object pairing. This connects behavior and affect to reference.
The PDF provides the demonstration title rather than its original video. The teaching point is the use of the speaker's intention as evidence about a word's meaning.

development2.title: The whole-object assumption
paragraphs: The **whole-object assumption** is a default interpretation that a new noun names an entire object rather than one of its parts, properties, or actions.
It narrows the mapping problem immediately. A novel word spoken near an unfamiliar toy is initially linked to the toy as a whole instead of every visible feature separately.
A default is a starting preference, not an unchangeable rule. More informative contextual or linguistic evidence can support a different meaning.

development2.title: Mutual exclusivity
paragraphs: **Mutual exclusivity** is a default tendency to map a new word onto an object without an already known name. If one object is familiar and another unnamed, the unfamiliar one is a plausible referent.
The strategy reduces competition among possible mappings. Existing vocabulary becomes evidence about where a new label is likely to belong.

The lecture places its emergence in the later portion of the second year. The essential idea is the inference from known naming relations, rather than a requirement that an object literally can never have more than one label.

development2.title: Applying mutual exclusivity in a choice
paragraphs: Suppose a known object and an unfamiliar object are available when a novel label is requested. The strategy favors the object without a known label.
This follows from treating the familiar object's existing name as a reason to seek another referent. The choice therefore uses vocabulary knowledge to solve a new mapping problem.
The source page introduces a demonstration. Its concept can be understood through the decision structure even though the original video is not embedded in the uploaded PDF.

development2.title: From short utterances to constructions
paragraphs: Menn distinguishes a collection of relevant words, memorized formulas, productive combinations, and stable constructions. The same short utterance can fit different explanations depending on its context.
Up, pick you up, and mommy up differ in length but do not by themselves reveal the child's full system. A formula can be reproduced without flexible control of all its parts.
Context and generalization help distinguish these possibilities. The goal is to determine whether a child can use a pattern productively beyond one familiar routine.

development2.title: Comprehension can exceed production
paragraphs: Children producing only one word at a time can already use basic transitive word order in comprehension. Their spoken output is therefore an incomplete measure of their structural knowledge.
In a sentence–scene comparison, word order can specify which participant acts and which receives the action. A child need not produce the full sentence to show that distinction.
This separates linguistic understanding from production demands. Short utterances do not automatically imply that the child has no representation of relations involving several words.

development2.title: Gertner: a novel verb tests generalization
paragraphs: Two-year-olds heard a sentence such as the duck is gorping the bunny while viewing novel actions with reversed actor–recipient roles. **Gorping** is unfamiliar, so its meaning cannot simply be recalled from a known phrase.
Children looked longer at the action in which the duck acted on the bunny. The transitive word-order pattern identified the roles even with a new verb.
This is evidence of generalization beyond memorized utterances. Their MLU (mean length of utterance) is around two. Understanding the relation can exceed a short production such as duck gorp bunny.

l1-critical.title: When first-language experience occurs
paragraphs: An **L1** is a first language. Studies of delayed access to any language ask whether the timing of early experience changes later attainment.
The lecture first uses visual development to explain experience-dependent organization, then applies the timing question to brain injury and delayed language exposure.

l1-critical.title: Critical versus sensitive periods
paragraphs: A strict **critical period** has a discrete onset and offset, with relevant learning confined to that interval. Outside it, the proposed system is insensitive to that learning experience.
A **sensitive** or **optimal period** instead makes some ages especially favorable while allowing learning at other ages. Its timing and effectiveness may also depend on experience.

Evidence of an age advantage does not by itself choose between these descriptions. Continued improvement after the favored window fits a sensitive-period account more naturally than an absolute cutoff.

l1-critical.title: Amblyopia and early visual input
paragraphs: **Amblyopia** is poor vision in an eye despite normal peripheral function at the time it is assessed. Early abnormal input can leave a lasting cortical consequence.
Strabismus misaligns the eyes, a cataract clouds input, and anisometropia gives the eyes different optical properties. Each can disrupt the normal relationship between the inputs during development.
Repairing the initial condition does not necessarily restore ordinary vision. The lasting impairment reflects how the brain organized itself while the input was abnormal.

l1-critical.title: Competition between the eyes
paragraphs: Inputs from the eyes compete for cortical representation. If one eye supplies abnormal input, the other can gain an increasing representational advantage.
