Restoring the disadvantaged eye's physical function does not immediately reverse that organization. The stronger input continues to dominate the existing competitive system.
The sequence links a temporary early disturbance to a persistent later outcome. What matters is not only what information arrives now but the representation established by earlier experience.

l1-critical.title: Why patch the stronger eye?
paragraphs: Patching the better eye reduces its competitive advantage. The weaker eye then has more opportunity to drive processing and benefit from the brain's plasticity.
The treatment is generally more effective early in development. Later in childhood the already-established imbalance can be harder to alter through this intervention.
The mechanism is experience-dependent rebalancing. Covering the stronger eye does not repair the weaker eye's optics directly; it changes how the cortical system uses the competing inputs.

l1-critical.title: Adult perceptual learning in amblyopia
paragraphs: Levi and Polat examined intensive practice in adults with amblyopia. Repeated psychophysical training in the affected eye improved task performance and aspects of visual function.
The graph relates performance to extended training, showing that substantial exposure can change an adult system that had developed abnormally. The relevant comparison is improvement with practice.

Adult plasticity is therefore reduced or differently accessed, rather than necessarily absent. A sensitive-period description accommodates both an early advantage and later learning under suitable conditions.

l1-critical.title: Game-based visual training
paragraphs: The cited work examines video-game training in adult amblyopia. Game performance engages repeated visual discrimination and attention in the affected system.
Its place in the argument is adult experience producing visual change. The example extends the idea of training beyond one narrowly repeated laboratory judgment.
The conceptual connection is to plasticity after the optimal developmental period. Improvement later in life distinguishes an especially effective early window from a permanent end to all learning.

l1-critical.title: From temporary deprivation to lasting organization
paragraphs: An early disturbance can change the experience-dependent organization of the visual system. Persistent poor function is a consequence of that developmental history.
Treatment works most readily within an earlier window, but appropriately structured adult training can also improve function. The timing and the nature of experience both matter.
Amblyopia therefore illustrates a **sensitive period** with competitive dynamics. It supplies a concrete mechanism to consider when interpreting age effects in other developing systems.

l1-critical.title: Connecting visual development to language
paragraphs: The language question is whether experience at particular ages is especially important for building an effective language system. Lenneberg connected this possibility to developmental neurology.
Deprivation cases ask what happens when accessible language is absent early. Delayed sign-language access provides a different kind of evidence from histories of severe neglect.
These comparisons concern access to a usable language, not simply whether someone has heard speech. A child needs input the developing system can actually perceive and learn from.

l1-critical.title: Lenneberg's developmental synthesis
paragraphs: Lenneberg linked stage-like language milestones with the changing brain. An orderly developmental sequence made a maturational contribution plausible.

A **maturational** account attributes change partly to the organism's biological development. The proposal was that the ability to acquire language might open and close in relation to that development.
The evidence combined linguistic milestones and neurological observations. The important causal question is which changes enable early learning and which reduce later reorganization.

l1-critical.title: The proposed opening of the learning window
paragraphs: Early brain-development data largely came from postmortem tissue. Measures such as neuronal size and packing density changed rapidly during early childhood.

Lenneberg considered these changes potentially permissive for the beginning of language acquisition. A permissive change enables a process; it need not specify every word or rule that will be learned.

The plotted age coverage is sparse, including a large gap between childhood and adulthood. The proposal links biological change and learning capacity without a continuously sampled developmental record.

l1-critical.title: Recovery and cerebral dominance
paragraphs: Children can show substantial language development after very early damage, including removal of a hemisphere to treat severe epilepsy. Comparable adult injury has very different consequences.
Lenneberg related the contrast to **cerebral dominance**, the developing asymmetry of language organization between hemispheres. Earlier organization was proposed to allow more flexibility.

The prediction is that developmental state changes how readily other tissue supports language. The evidence concerns reorganization after injury, rather than directly measuring one switch that ends language learning.

l1-critical.title: Perinatal stroke outcomes
paragraphs: A **perinatal stroke** occurs around birth. Children with such injuries often have better language outcomes than adults with comparable damage.
Better does not necessarily mean fully typical. Studies show early deficits after injury to either hemisphere and later outcomes that may remain in a low-normal range.
Early plasticity can support substantial function while leaving persistent costs. The comparison distinguishes relative resilience from complete compensation.

l1-critical.title: Genie and delayed access to language
paragraphs: Genie experienced severe deprivation and abuse with extremely restricted early linguistic interaction. The case offered an opportunity to observe language learning after unusually delayed access.

Her later learning involved vocabulary, comprehension, and production developing at different rates. These components must be considered separately rather than summarized as language present or absent.

The central timing question is whether the delayed first-language history especially affects grammar. The severe deprivation history is also part of what makes this case different from ordinary late instruction.

l1-critical.title: What Genie learned
paragraphs: Genie developed comprehension of many words, some prepositions, and aspects of morphology. Plurals were a relative area of success in the observations described.
**Morphology** concerns meaningful word parts, such as plural marking. Understanding a plural distinction is more than recognizing an isolated object name.
The case therefore shows substantial later learning. The pattern is uneven: acquiring vocabulary and selected grammatical relations does not imply that the full system develops at the same rate.

l1-critical.title: Production and grammar developed more slowly
paragraphs: Genie's production remained far behind comprehension. Some comprehension advantage occurs in typical development, but her early punishment for making sounds also bears directly on speaking.
Grammatical abilities grew much more slowly than vocabulary. The contrast is between components of acquisition rather than a total inability to learn anything after childhood.
This difference made the case influential in discussion of L1 timing. A later learner could acquire many meanings while still struggling with the productive organization of sentences.

l1-critical.title: Interpreting the delayed-learning pattern
paragraphs: The grammar–vocabulary disparity is consistent with the idea that early experience is especially important for first-language grammar. It is the pattern of learning, not simply the age at observation, that motivates this interpretation.
Genie also had a history of severe abuse, disrupted social development, and uncertain prior capacities. Those factors affect both the input and the learning situation.

The observation period ended when funding stopped. The case provides evidence about observed development over that interval, while other delayed-language populations help test which aspects of the pattern generalize.

l1-critical.title: Mayberry: late L1 versus late L2 in sign
paragraphs: Some deaf children encounter an accessible first language only when sign language becomes available later. A comparison group learned spoken language earlier and later acquired sign after becoming deaf.
The groups may begin sign at similar ages but differ in prior language experience. Late first-language learners have greater difficulty than learners who already established another language.
This separates age of learning a particular language from age of access to any language. Early linguistic experience provides a foundation whose effects can persist into later learning and adulthood.

l1-critical.title: What the timing evidence has in common
paragraphs: Brain-injury recovery differs greatly between childhood and adulthood. Delayed first-language access is also associated with persistent difficulties, especially in complex language learning.
Simply withholding input does not appear to preserve an indefinitely open first-language window. Time passes and the system develops even when normal experience is missing.

These findings support an important role for early accessible language. The sensitive-period distinction remains useful because later learning can occur without reproducing the outcome of early acquisition.

l1-critical.title: From first-language timing to L2
paragraphs: Second-language learning lets the timing question be examined in many more people. Learners already possess a language but differ in when and how they encounter another.
The next comparison therefore asks whether early L1 experience preserves later capacity, or whether maturation changes learning even after a first language is established.

l1-critical.title: Further examples of deprivation and plasticity
paragraphs: The source lists films and further material related to Genie, unusual language histories, and plasticity. These extend the theme of what early experience changes.

The common question remains whether later experience can restore a function, build a new one, or reveal residual learning. These are different outcomes and should be distinguished when connecting a case to a sensitive-period account.

sentence.title: Understanding sentences while they unfold
paragraphs: **Sentence processing** assigns structure and meaning as words arrive. A listener or reader often has to choose among several possible relationships before the sentence is complete.
The central issue is how syntactic preferences, meaning, context, and expectations interact. Reading times, eye movements, actions, and brain responses reveal parts of that process.

sentence.title: The horse raced past the barn fell
paragraphs: The sentence can mean that the horse that was raced past the barn subsequently fell. Raced past the barn modifies which horse is being discussed; fell is the main predicate.
An initial interpretation instead treats raced as the main verb. On reaching fell, that analysis leaves no straightforward place for the new main event.
Adding that was after horse makes the modifying structure explicit. The difficulty therefore concerns resolving a **reduced relative clause**, not the impossibility of expressing the intended event.

sentence.title: What a garden path is
paragraphs: A **garden path** occurs when an initially attractive interpretation becomes incompatible with later input. The reader must revise the earlier structural assignment to continue.
In the horse example, the early main-verb reading of raced is the tempting path. The later fell forces raced to be reinterpreted as part of a modifying clause.
The experience shows that comprehension is incremental. The system commits enough to an interpretation during the sentence that later evidence can produce a measurable cost of reanalysis.

sentence.title: A parser under memory and time constraints
paragraphs: A **parser** builds a structural analysis connecting the words of a sentence. The initial tree assigns raced to the main verb position and treats the following material accordingly.
Maintaining every possible tree would demand memory and time. An efficient system might prefer a simpler analysis and revise it only when later evidence makes that necessary.
The account explains a garden path through a processing strategy. The sentence is grammatical under another structure, but the parser initially chooses a different one.

sentence.title: Minimal attachment
paragraphs: **Minimal attachment** favors the analysis requiring fewer structural nodes. In the horse sentence, treating raced as the main verb initially builds a smaller tree than introducing a reduced relative clause.
When fell arrives, the smaller analysis fails. The correct structure has additional organization connecting the horse to a modifying clause before its main verb.
The proposed cause of difficulty is therefore a preference for structural economy. Reanalysis requires undoing the earlier economical choice and constructing the larger alternative.

sentence.title: Late closure and dynamite
paragraphs: **Late closure** favors attaching incoming material to the structure currently being processed. A phrase tends to continue the current clause or phrase when a grammatical analysis permits it.
In the burglar blew open the safe with the dynamite, the final phrase can attach to the action. Dynamite then specifies the instrument used to blow the safe open.
An alternative attachment makes the phrase describe the safe. The experiment compares interpretations of a locally ambiguous phrase rather than sentences with different words in every position.

sentence.title: Why jewels create a processing cost
paragraphs: With the jewels can describe the safe's contents, but jewels are an unlikely instrument for blowing it open. The plausible meaning therefore favors noun attachment over the initially preferred action attachment.
Reading-time and eye-movement measures show a cost when the sensible analysis conflicts with the preferred structure. The system briefly entertains a less sensible relation and then revises it.
This is an argument about the order of information use. A syntactic preference can guide the initial analysis before plausibility redirects the interpretation.

sentence.title: An autonomous structural parser
paragraphs: An **autonomous parser** initially computes syntactic structure using its own structural preferences. Meaning is not the primary determinant of that first analysis.
Minimal attachment and late closure provide efficient defaults. They avoid maintaining many complete alternatives by choosing an economical path until a problem appears.

The account resembles the staged lumber-mill model: one kind of operation supplies an analysis for another to evaluate. Experiments then ask whether nonstructural information can affect the earliest choices themselves.

sentence.title: Reduced relatives are not always difficult
paragraphs: Some reduced-relative sentences are easy to understand despite having the supposedly demanding structural form. Their words and likely meanings make the modifying interpretation natural.

MacDonald, Perlmutter, and Seidenberg argue that semantic cues and learned distributional regularities influence parsing from early on. The same abstract construction can receive different support in different contexts.
A structure's existence therefore does not uniquely predict its processing difficulty. The frequency and plausibility of its components can change how strongly the competing analyses are activated.

sentence.title: Why the example table matters
paragraphs: The table collects reduced-relative examples that readers encounter without an overwhelming garden path. Several come from discussions that otherwise use reduced relatives to support autonomous parsing.
Their shared structure is compatible with different experienced difficulty. This focuses attention on lexical and contextual differences instead of treating the construction as uniformly hard.
The comparison motivates a **constraint-based** view: several partial sources of information favor or disfavor an analysis as the input unfolds.

sentence.title: Research reported and the arrested burglar
paragraphs: In recent research reported by, research is unlikely to perform the reporting, and reported often occurs in modifying constructions. Meaning and learned usage favor a reduced-relative interpretation.
A burglar is also more likely to be arrested than to perform an arrest. A policeman has a stronger association with acting as the arresting agent, increasing competition for the alternative analysis.
These differences concern **lexical statistics** and world knowledge. They can make two structurally similar sentences differ in how readily the correct analysis emerges.

sentence.title: Spivey: an apple, a towel, and a box
paragraphs: Participants saw an apple on a towel, another towel, a box, and other objects. They heard put the apple on the towel in the box while their eye movements were measured.
On the towel can first sound like a destination for put. The correct instruction instead uses it to identify the apple, with in the box specifying the final destination.
Looks to the empty towel reveal a temporary destination interpretation. The final action can be correct even though the eye trace records an earlier competing plan.

sentence.title: The one-apple display
paragraphs: With only one apple available, the noun already identifies the target. A following location phrase is less needed to distinguish it from another apple.
The empty towel can therefore attract looks as a possible destination while the instruction unfolds. Later in the box resolves the required movement.
The visual scene supplies information about what needs specifying. The ambiguity is not solely a property of the spoken words detached from their task context.

sentence.title: Adding a second apple
paragraphs: When two apples are present, on the towel becomes useful for identifying which apple to move. The phrase now has an immediate referential purpose.
Listeners make fewer looks to the irrelevant destination towel than in the one-apple situation. The spoken sentence remains the same while the visual context changes.
This supports early use of **referential context**. The need to distinguish objects can change which structural interpretation is favored during processing.

sentence.title: What the context comparison shows
paragraphs: The eye-movement comparison measures the temporary attraction of the wrong destination in one- and two-referent scenes. Its reduction with two apples shows context changing the evolving interpretation.

A purely syntactic default would not straightforwardly predict a different early preference from the same string solely because another apple is present. The contextual distinction is informative before the sentence ends.

Syntax and pragmatics therefore interact during comprehension. **Pragmatics** concerns how an expression serves the communicative situation, including why a speaker would specify one apple's location.

sentence.title: Mouse trajectories and competing actions
paragraphs: Mouse tracking records the developing movement toward a response. A curved or diverted path can reveal competing interpretations that influence the action before it is completed.
The one-referent and two-referent contexts affect these trajectories, just as they affect eye movements. Ambiguity changes the execution of the action rather than only a retrospective report.
The method measures time course through movement. A correct endpoint need not mean there was never competition on the way to it.

sentence.title: Brain responses to structural expectations
paragraphs: **Event-related potentials**, or ERPs, are brain electrical responses averaged relative to a defined event, such as a word appearing. Their timing helps identify when a manipulation affects processing.
Syntax experiments compare a word in an expected versus an unexpected category position. The physical word and its sentence context together determine what counts as a violation.
An early response provides evidence of rapid expectation sensitivity. Explaining its mechanism requires examining both grammatical structure and properties of the word's form.

sentence.title: The: starting the incremental sentence
paragraphs: The begins a noun phrase and creates expectations about what kinds of material can follow. No complete sentence meaning is available yet.

In word-by-word presentation, the response to each new item is interpreted relative to the material already seen. This lets the experiment measure the unfolding process instead of only the final judgment.
The developing prediction is provisional. Later words can specify, satisfy, or conflict with what the earlier context made likely.

sentence.title: Pizza: establishing the noun phrase
paragraphs: Pizza supplies the noun following the determiner. The reader can now construct a noun phrase referring to a particular kind of entity.
This is still not a complete proposition. The next words must establish what is said about the pizza and how the remaining sentence fits together.
Incremental presentation separates recognizing a word from integrating it into an evolving structure. The same word can be easy to recognize while its grammatical continuation remains open.

sentence.title: Was: opening a new structural expectation
paragraphs: Was changes the developing expectations for the predicate. It can participate in constructions describing a state or a passive event, depending on what follows.
The reader uses the emerging phrase to predict compatible continuations. Those predictions need not wait until a whole sentence is visible.
This stage prepares the later violation comparison. An unexpected item is defined by its relationship to the structure established so far.

sentence.title: In: introducing a prepositional phrase
paragraphs: In introduces a prepositional relation. A continuation can specify the location or context associated with the pizza.
The preposition changes which forms are expected next. It invites a phrase of an appropriate category rather than an arbitrary sequence of recognizable words.
A category-sensitive response therefore depends on the prior context. Recognizing in also reorganizes predictions about the next part of the sentence.

sentence.title: The: expecting a noun after the preposition
paragraphs: The pizza was in the now strongly sets up a noun-phrase continuation after the preposition. A noun would complete the immediate determiner–noun relation.
This is a specific expectation about grammatical category. It is different from merely guessing a semantically related word such as a common pizza topping.
The ERP comparison asks what happens when the next item conflicts with that prepared category and whether its visible form contributes to the response.

sentence.title: Eaten: a word-category violation
paragraphs: Eaten does not supply the ordinary noun required by the immediately preceding in the sequence. The words are individually recognizable, but their combination disrupts the expected structure.
The crucial event occurs when the violating item arrives. The reader can detect the mismatch before evaluating a long, completed passage.
This separates lexical familiarity from structural fit. Knowing a word does not ensure that it belongs in the position where it is encountered.

sentence.title: The early left anterior negativity
paragraphs: The **ELAN**, early left anterior negativity, is an ERP effect reported for word-category violations, with an early timing around 100–200 milliseconds. The name describes its timing, polarity, and scalp distribution.
Sequences such as the pizza was in the eaten place an item where its grammatical category does not fit. Researchers compare responses with category-appropriate continuations.
The timing motivated interest in rapid syntactic processing. Whether the effect identifies an autonomous grammar computation depends on what physical cues distinguish the compared words.

sentence.title: Early visual predictions and form typicality
paragraphs: Dikker and colleagues related early responses to properties of written word forms. A context predicting a verb can also prepare visual patterns associated with verb-like words.
A mismatch between the expected form and the displayed form can influence visual cortex rapidly. A very early category-related effect can therefore include perceptual prediction.

**Form typicality** means how characteristic a word's physical pattern is of a class. The question shifts from category labels alone to how grammatical expectations connect with learned form statistics.

sentence.title: Perches and needs can change category
paragraphs: In the bird perches seem easy to install, perches is a noun referring to objects. In the bird perches comfortably, it functions as a verb.
Similarly, student needs can refer to requirements or describe what a student requires. Context changes the grammatical role without changing the ambiguous word's spelling.
These contrasts help separate the form's usual category associations from its role in a particular sentence. A word can be statistically noun-like while functioning as a verb, or the reverse.

sentence.title: Noun-like and verb-like forms
paragraphs: Perches is classified as more noun-like in the form-based comparison; needs is more verb-like. Those tendencies are statistical associations rather than an inability to use each form in the other category.
The sentence pairs place them in contexts requiring different categories. The analysis asks whether response patterns follow contextual role, typical form, or their interaction.
This makes prediction concrete: an unexpected category with a strongly incompatible form may be detected differently from one whose spelling provides little category evidence.

sentence.title: Comparing form-based and syntactic expectations
paragraphs: The figure compares how words' form properties relate to the noun and verb categories being tested. The sentence contexts independently establish the required grammatical role.
A mismatch can therefore be varied while preserving a meaningful distinction between form typicality and sentence structure. Both contribute information available to the reader.
The logic is to identify what drives the early response. If form matters, a category violation need not produce the same effect for every noun or verb.

sentence.title: When a category violation produces the early effect
paragraphs: The early effect appeared where a noun's category was supported by morphological marking or statistical form information. Neutral nouns without strong category cues did not show the same effect.
**Morphological marking** supplies a meaningful form cue; statistical nouniness comes from the patterns shared by many noun forms. Both are physically available when the written word appears.
The result connects the early response to predicted physical form. It does not reduce all syntax to spelling; it explains why the earliest measured mismatch can depend on learned visual properties.

sentence.title: Four sentences, four connected lessons
paragraphs: Colorless green ideas sleep furiously separates grammatical organization from sensible meaning. The horse sentence shows that locally preferred structures can create garden paths.
Put the apple on the towel in the box shows early contextual influence. The bird perches example links grammatical expectations to the physical form of the upcoming word.

Together these cases describe incremental interpretation shaped by several constraints. A sentence's structure matters, while its words, scene, and expected forms help determine how that structure is reached.

sentence.title: From parsing to aphasia
paragraphs: The aphasia material asks how the operations used in sentence comprehension change after brain injury. Structural ambiguity and role assignment provide useful test contrasts.
The connection is experimental: choosing sentences that separate syntax, plausibility, and processing demands makes it possible to explain specific patterns of comprehension difficulty.

l2-learning.title: Learning a second language
paragraphs: An **L2** is a second language learned after another language is established. Learning draws on existing conceptual skills and linguistic representations while adapting to a new system.
The central topics are transfer, competition between languages, and what happens when a previously used language stops receiving input.

l2-learning.title: Learning speed versus ultimate attainment
paragraphs: Adults often learn more quickly at the beginning of L2 instruction. They already possess conceptual knowledge, learning strategies, and an established language that can support the new task.
**Ultimate attainment** is the level reached after extended learning. Earlier learners more often reach native-like outcomes even though they may initially progress more slowly.
These measures answer different questions. A child advantage in eventual attainment does not imply that adults learn fewer words in every early lesson.

l2-learning.title: Conceptual knowledge supports later learners
paragraphs: A first-language learner is also developing concepts such as spatial relationships and events. An older L2 learner already has much of that knowledge available.
The later learner can focus on how the new language expresses familiar relations. This reduces some demands compared with learning both the concepts and their linguistic expression.
Existing language also shapes attention and expectations. The same prior experience that helps with one feature can interfere with a feature organized differently in L2.

l2-learning.title: Positive and negative transfer
paragraphs: **Transfer** is using L1 processes and representations in L2. It is positive when the existing pattern fits the new language and negative when it creates a misleading expectation.
Similar words or structures can reduce the amount that must be learned. Incompatible sound categories, agreement rules, or word meanings can instead create persistent errors.
Transfer is therefore a relation between two systems. The question is which specific previously learned mapping is being reused and whether it matches the target language.

l2-learning.title: Dental and retroflex contrasts
paragraphs: Hindi distinguishes dental and retroflex consonants that English listeners may initially interpret using one alveolar category. **Place of articulation** describes where a consonant is produced.
Mapping both L2 sounds onto the same L1 category makes their difference less salient. The learner must establish a distinction that was not required in the same way by English.
This is negative phonetic transfer. Familiar categorization helps recognize speech generally but can merge two sounds that must be separated to distinguish L2 words.

l2-learning.title: Learning classifiers
paragraphs: Chinese classifiers depend on properties associated with the noun. Different nouns require different classifier choices in relevant constructions.
English determiner use does not demand that same system of semantic sorting. An English learner must start attending to distinctions that ordinary L1 grammar did not require in that position.
The transfer problem is therefore not just remembering another short word. It involves learning which noun properties control a grammatical choice.

l2-learning.title: Grammatical gender and agreement
paragraphs: **Grammatical gender** assigns nouns to classes that affect related words. It is distinct from social gender and need not reflect a noun's real-world properties.
Pronouns, adjectives, and some verb forms may have to agree with a noun's grammatical class. French synonyms can belong to different classes even when they refer to similar things.
A learner must acquire both class membership and the consequences for agreement. L1 habits can interfere when the first language does not organize those dependencies similarly.

l2-learning.title: Cognates and borrowings
paragraphs: Similar words across languages can facilitate vocabulary learning. A **cognate** reflects shared historical origin, while a **loan word** comes from borrowing.
The lecture examples include recognizable European forms and Japanese adaptations of borrowed vocabulary. Similarity can provide an initial connection between a new form and an already known meaning.

This is positive transfer: prior representations reduce uncertainty. The useful claim concerns a helpful relation between form and meaning, not a guarantee that every familiar-looking form shares its meaning.

l2-learning.title: False friends
paragraphs: A word that resembles an L1 form can have a different meaning. Spanish embarazado means pregnant, not embarrassed. Its familiar-looking form can therefore produce a confident but mistaken interpretation.
The bias is understandable: many cross-language similarities are useful, so an existing word is quickly activated by a similar L2 form. The error occurs when the meaning relation does not match.
**False friends** therefore expose negative lexical transfer. Learning requires distinguishing useful correspondences from misleading ones rather than avoiding L1 knowledge altogether.

l2-learning.title: De Groot and Keijzer: paired-associate learning
paragraphs: Dutch speakers learned pairs linking familiar Dutch words to invented foreign-like forms. The pairs varied in cognate similarity and in whether their meanings were concrete or abstract.
Participants studied the associations and later took a retention test after a week without training. This separates initial learning from how much remains later.

The design tests whether form similarity contributes from the beginning of learning. The made-up forms allow a defined manipulation rather than relying only on participants' prior experience with a real L2.

l2-learning.title: Cognate advantages in learning and retention
paragraphs: Cognate-like pairs were acquired more rapidly and retained better. Session 4 follows a week without practice, so its performance measures persistence rather than another immediate study trial.
Form similarity can provide a bridge between a new label and an existing lexical representation. That bridge can help both establishing and retrieving the association.

The table also contains concreteness differences, but the stated lecture emphasis is the cognate effect. The important result is that similarity helps from the earliest stages, not only after extensive fluency.

l2-learning.title: Why test production as well as recognition?
paragraphs: A **receptive** test supplies the new form and asks for the familiar meaning. A cognate can sometimes be guessed from its resemblance even without successful learning.
A **productive** or expressive test asks the learner to generate the new form from the familiar word. The answer is not fully supplied by the prompt.

A benefit in productive testing therefore provides stronger evidence of a learned mapping. It addresses whether participants can retrieve the new representation rather than merely recognize a transparent clue.

l2-learning.title: Reading immediate and delayed recall
paragraphs: The table separates productive from receptive recall and immediate from delayed tests. Cognates outperform noncognates across these comparisons, with less forgetting over the delay.
Concrete items are also retained better than abstract ones in the displayed data. This is a second factor, so it should not be confused with cognate status.

Productive success matters particularly because it requires retrieving a foreign-like form. The pattern supports both initial acquisition and retention advantages rather than an effect limited to guessing familiar meanings.

l2-learning.title: Are both languages active during L2 recognition?
paragraphs: The research question is whether an L2 word activates similar L1 words even when the task is conducted in L2. A visual-world display can make those potential competitors observable.
A listener hears a target and looks among objects. Additional looks to an object whose L1 name overlaps with the input indicate cross-language competition.
The task therefore tests selective language access during ordinary word identification. Knowing which language is being used may not prevent all activation in the other lexicon.

l2-learning.title: Using eye movements to measure competition
paragraphs: McMurray's bear–pear task showed that eye movements reveal partial competition hidden by the final click. The competitor becomes more attractive as acoustic input grows ambiguous.
Bilingual experiments use the same logic with a different kind of competitor. A picture can compete because its name in another language resembles the spoken target.
The measure concerns activation during processing. A correct L2 response can coexist with temporary attraction to an L1-linked object.

l2-learning.title: Cohort activation within a language
paragraphs: A **cohort** consists of words compatible with the beginning of a spoken form. Early input activates more than one candidate, and later sounds reduce the competition.
In a visual-world display, looks to a same-onset competitor rise and then decline as the target becomes clearer. The timing is important even if only one object is eventually selected.
This provides the baseline mechanism for the bilingual question. Cross-language cohorts extend onset competition beyond the language explicitly required by the task.

l2-learning.title: Marian and Spivey's cross-language competitor
paragraphs: Native Russian speakers processed English targets while viewing objects. A target such as speaker overlaps in sound with the Russian name for matches, making the matches picture a potential competitor.
The picture's English name need not resemble the target. The phonological overlap arises through the other language.

If looks increase relative to an unrelated control, recognition is not fully restricted to English candidates. The experiment can compare within-language and between-language competition in the same setting.

l2-learning.title: Competition during L2 processing
paragraphs: In the English task, listeners looked at both English and Russian-name competitors. With one competitor present, within- and between-language competition were comparable in the reported conditions.
When both appeared together, the English competitor attracted more looks, but the Russian competitor still exceeded the control. Competition from the other language did not disappear.
The result supports nonselective activation during L2 recognition in this population. The task language shapes competition without perfectly isolating one lexicon.

l2-learning.title: The asymmetry during L1 processing
paragraphs: When the native Russian speakers performed the task in Russian, the English competitor did not show a statistically reliable advantage over the control in the reported data.
This differs from the L2 task, where Russian-name competitors attracted looks. The comparison asks about the direction and strength of cross-language influence.

An asymmetrical connection account can explain why L1 intrudes more into L2 than the reverse for these learners. The small plotted difference is not equivalent to evidence for a reliable competitor effect.

l2-learning.title: The Revised Hierarchical Model
paragraphs: The **Revised Hierarchical Model** links L1 words, L2 words, and shared concepts. The L1 lexicon is larger and more strongly connected to concepts in the learner configuration shown.
L2 words have relatively strong links toward their L1 counterparts. Such a path is reinforced by learning a new word through a familiar translation.
Unequal link strengths make directional predictions. Activating L2 can engage L1 more readily than activating L1 engages L2 in this particular configuration.

l2-learning.title: How a competitor gains conceptual support
paragraphs: The English input can activate an overlapping Russian word. That lexical activation can in turn support the corresponding concept, making its pictured referent attract attention.
Connections between words and concepts allow activation to circulate. Once the matches representation is partially involved, feedback can maintain its competition during the English task.

Weaker access from L1 into L2 helps explain the opposite-task asymmetry. The mechanism concerns routes and strengths of activation, rather than a claim that the two picture meanings must themselves be similar.

l2-learning.title: Balanced bilinguals still have interacting systems
paragraphs: A **balanced bilingual** has relatively strong access to both languages. In an interactive account, stronger links do not necessarily eliminate competition.

If both languages connect effectively to shared concepts, activation and inhibitory control can be engaged across languages repeatedly. The person is not simply switching between two entirely isolated monolingual systems.

This prediction motivated work on control outside language. The theoretical prediction of ongoing competition should be distinguished from treating every possible nonlinguistic advantage as already established by these eye-movement data.

l2-learning.title: What happens when L1 use stops?
paragraphs: The usual learning timeline adds L2 while L1 continues to be used. International adoption can instead sharply reduce or end contact with the original language.
This changes the input to an already organized system. Previously used connections may no longer be reinforced while the new language becomes dominant.
The question is whether L1 is still accessible, becomes harder to access, or leaves traces that can help later relearning. These outcomes require different tests.

l2-learning.title: Testing Korean adoptees in France
paragraphs: Adults adopted from Korea into French-speaking homes during childhood were tested for residual Korean knowledge. Their current language was French.
Comparison with monolingual French speakers asks whether early Korean exposure confers a remaining advantage. Different tasks can probe sounds, words, sentence memory, and brain responses.
The relevant history includes both early acquisition and later absence of input. This is a test of retention under a changed environment, not an ordinary classroom L2-learning trajectory.

l2-learning.title: The Korean three-way stop contrast
paragraphs: Korean distinguishes three kinds of stop consonants in the contrast shown. A listener must differentiate the language's phonetic categories rather than merely detect that two recordings differ.
Early Korean experience might be expected to support this distinction later, even after long use of French. The comparison therefore probes a specific possible trace of the earlier sound system.
Testing a well-defined contrast makes retention operational. Performance can be compared with listeners who have no comparable early Korean experience.

l2-learning.title: Ventureyra: no detected phonetic advantage
paragraphs: The adoptees did not outperform monolingual French listeners on the tested Korean contrasts. Their early experience did not produce an accessible advantage in that task.

The Korean comparison group supplies evidence that the contrast is measurable with relevant language experience. The key difference is therefore between retained current ability and a long-disused early history.
The finding concerns the tested phonetic discrimination. It motivates broader searches for residual knowledge rather than assuming that one negative task exhausts every possible form of retention.

l2-learning.title: Pallier's broader behavioral tests
paragraphs: Pallier and colleagues tested language identification, Korean word translations, and detection of repeated excerpts in recorded sentences. These target different potential remnants of L1 experience.
The adoptees again did not show an advantage over monolingual French listeners. The tests sought any accessible trace rather than only performance on a demanding grammar test.

Agreement across several measures strengthens the observation of little detectable residual knowledge under those conditions. It also distinguishes current access from what later retraining might reveal.

l2-learning.title: Brain responses to the current language
paragraphs: French activated familiar temporal and frontal language regions in the adoptees. Their current language therefore recruited a conventional language network.

Contrasting French with Korean did not reveal the predicted residual Korean-processing difference between the groups. The imaging comparison converges with the behavioral tests' lack of a detected advantage.

The result shows substantial reorganization with changed language experience. Brain responses and behavioral performance address related aspects of which language representations are currently effective.

l2-learning.title: Competition as an account of replacement
paragraphs: Connections supporting a language gain strength through use. When L1 is no longer activated and L2 dominates experience, the competitive balance can shift toward the new system.

The lecture compares this with experience-dependent competition in visual development. A previously advantaged representation can lose effective access when another pattern is consistently reinforced.
This provides a process for apparent replacement. It does not require a whole language to disappear instantaneously when adoption occurs; changing use alters the system over time.

l2-learning.title: Retention can become visible through relearning
paragraphs: Failure to detect a skill in an initial task need not settle whether early experience influences future learning. A later learning phase can test how readily the relevant patterns return.

**Unmasking** means making an earlier influence observable under conditions that were not present in the first test. The next example examines people with childhood exposure who later studied the language.
The question changes from what can be performed now to what prior experience contributes to subsequent acquisition. Those are related but distinct measures of retention.

l2-learning.title: Au: childhood Spanish overhearers
paragraphs: Students who often overheard Spanish as children but did not learn to speak it later took classroom Spanish. Their childhood exposure preceded comparable later instruction.

Performance after later learning can reveal benefits not obvious in initial fluent production. The early experience may preserve useful phonological information even without a previously spoken vocabulary.
The comparison addresses residual learning through later training. Childhood hearing and childhood speaking are different histories, so the type of early experience must be specified.

l2-learning.title: Apparent replacement and residual knowledge
paragraphs: The Korean adoption tasks showed little accessible early-language advantage, while the overhearer work indicates that early exposure can affect later learning. These outcomes probe different forms of retention.
A representation may be difficult to use spontaneously but still influence relearning. Current proficiency and learning efficiency should therefore be measured separately.
The synthesis connects competition with persistence. New-language dominance can coexist with early traces whose contribution becomes visible only under another learning condition.

l2-learning.title: Why language histories matter
paragraphs: Korean exposure in France differs from Spanish exposure in Los Angeles. Continued opportunities to hear a language, family use, cognates, and a shared writing system can change later outcomes.
These are mechanisms affecting maintenance and transfer, not interchangeable background details. A heritage-language environment can reinforce connections that complete absence of input does not.
Comparing learner groups requires tracking those histories. The effect attributed to early experience also depends on what happened between that experience and the eventual test.

l2-sensitive.title: Age and second-language attainment
paragraphs: L2 sensitive-period research asks how the age of learning relates to eventual proficiency. Learners already possess an L1, making this a different comparison from delayed first-language access.
Age of arrival, task demands, transfer, and experience all contribute to interpreting the data. The central skill is explaining the pattern rather than assuming that one correlation names its cause.

l2-sensitive.title: Lenneberg's laterality proposal
paragraphs: Lenneberg connected language-learning capacity to the development of cerebral dominance. The proposal combined milestones with evidence of greater early resilience after brain injury.
A laterality account makes maturation part of the learning explanation. As organization changes, the opportunities for reorganization may also change.
L2 data test the broader timing prediction in learners with different ages of onset. They do not directly measure cerebral dominance simply by measuring grammar accuracy.

l2-sensitive.title: Why L2 provides a larger comparison
paragraphs: Severely delayed L1 cases are unusual and often involve complicated histories. L2 acquisition occurs at many ages in much larger populations.
Comparing later attainment across these learners can reveal age-related patterns. It also adds variation in prior language, instruction, and amount of experience.
The research question becomes whether a timing effect remains informative about learning capacity when those histories and the measurement task are considered.

l2-sensitive.title: Johnson and Newport's study
paragraphs: Johnson and Newport compared English attainment among Chinese- and Korean-speaking learners who arrived at different ages. A grammaticality-judgment task assessed several English structures.
**Age of arrival**, or AOA, provides an index of when substantial exposure began. **Attainment** refers to the level eventually measured, rather than how quickly the first lesson was learned.
The proposed prediction was higher final proficiency after earlier arrival. The age pattern, including its shape before and after adolescence, is central to evaluating that proposal.

l2-sensitive.title: What a grammaticality judgment measures
paragraphs: Participants listened to recorded sentences and reported whether each was grammatical. The test was **untimed**, allowing reflection instead of requiring an immediate interpretation in conversation.
The example sets manipulate grammatical properties such as determiners, agreement, or questions. A correct response requires recognizing the particular contrast being tested.
This is a judgment about language, called **metalinguistic** performance. It can draw on explicit rules as well as the knowledge used during ordinary comprehension.

l2-sensitive.title: Reading the age-of-arrival scatterplots
paragraphs: Each point represents a learner's accuracy in relation to age of arrival. A downward relationship means that later arrival tends to accompany lower final judgment accuracy.
The early and late ranges must also be examined separately. An overall correlation can conceal a change from an age-related slope to broad variability without a clear slope.
Describe where near-native performance occurs and how the distribution changes. The plot's shape carries more information than a statement that younger is better.

l2-sensitive.title: Early high accuracy and later variability
paragraphs: Early arrivals often perform close to the native range, particularly those arriving in early childhood. Accuracy declines across later childhood arrival ages in the presented data.
Late arrivals show a wide spread of scores with little clear within-group relationship to age. Some perform much better than other late learners.
This is not a claim that late learners respond randomly or cannot learn grammar. The randomness concerns the scatter of attainment with respect to arrival age within that later range.

l2-sensitive.title: The sensitive-period interpretation
paragraphs: Johnson and Newport interpret the age-related early decline as a developmental reduction in ordinary language-learning capacity. The later scatter is attributed to greater dependence on individual learning abilities.
The explanation predicts both a timing relationship and a change in what determines success later. It is more specific than simply noting a mean difference between children and adults.

Some late acquisition remains possible. The pattern concerns typical ultimate attainment and its determinants rather than a strict statement that every postpubertal learner has zero sensitivity to language.

l2-sensitive.title: Exercise versus maturational-state hypotheses
paragraphs: The **exercise hypothesis** says early language use preserves the learning capacity: once exercised, it should remain available for subsequent acquisition. Without early use, it declines.

The **maturational-state hypothesis** says the capacity declines with maturation even if a first language was acquired normally. Established L1 knowledge would not fully preserve child-like L2 learning.
Lower attainment in older L2 learners who already used an L1 fits the second proposal more directly. The hypotheses differ in what early successful language acquisition is predicted to protect.

l2-sensitive.title: Explicit knowledge and task design
paragraphs: An untimed grammaticality judgment allows conscious reflection on learned rules. A person can deliberately evaluate a sentence rather than process it at ordinary conversational speed.
**Explicit knowledge** is knowledge available to conscious explanation or monitoring. **Implicit knowledge** can guide fluent performance without a verbalized rule.

A judgment task may combine these sources differently from spontaneous use. The measured age effect therefore belongs to a particular task and cannot automatically be assigned entirely to implicit grammar acquisition.

l2-sensitive.title: Education predicts untimed judgment performance
paragraphs: The lecture relates untimed GJT scores to years of formal L2 education. Schooling can strengthen knowledge of rules that are directly useful for deliberative judgments.
This fits the proposal that an untimed test draws substantially on explicit metalinguistic learning. A well-practiced rule explanation may help even when conversational performance differs.
The association makes task demands part of the attainment interpretation. Comparing timed, spontaneous, and untimed measures helps clarify which kind of knowledge is producing a score.

l2-sensitive.title: Transfer changes the age comparison
paragraphs: Languages differ in how many features map conveniently onto English. Similar vocabulary or constructions can support learning, while absent or incompatible features add difficulty.
Johnson and Newport's learners had Chinese or Korean as L1. Another language pairing can change the available transfer even at comparable ages of arrival.
An age effect must therefore be interpreted with the language pair in view. Maturation and prior representations both affect what an L2 learner must reorganize.

l2-sensitive.title: Not every construction is equally difficult
paragraphs: Progressive -ing and word order are relatively successful structures in the displayed results. Other properties, such as determiners, are harder for learners whose L1 lacks the relevant system.
Questions can be relatively successful for late learners despite emerging late in children's L1 development. L2 learning does not simply replay the entire L1 developmental order.
The pattern supports examining individual constructions. A total score combines different demands and different opportunities for transfer.

l2-sensitive.title: Birdsong and Molis: changing the language pair
paragraphs: The comparison with Spanish-speaking learners changes the relation between L1 and English. Their attainment distribution differs from the Chinese/Korean pattern used in the original argument.
Similarity between languages can change learning difficulty and the observed AOA relationship. The plots therefore test whether one age pattern generalizes across learner populations.
A maturational account must explain this dependence on language pairing as well as any overall earlier-learning advantage. Transfer contributes directly to the outcome being measured.

l2-sensitive.title: What a complete explanation must connect
paragraphs: Later onset is generally associated with lower L2 attainment, but the pattern depends on constructions, test demands, and language pairings. These factors change what a score represents.
Age also covaries with experience: instruction, opportunities for use, and immersion differ across histories. Separating those influences requires more than reading a single downward trend.
A useful explanation identifies the proposed mechanism and its prediction. Maturation, transfer, and explicit learning can each contribute, so their distinct effects must be matched to the evidence.

paragraphs: The source assigns the reading chapter next. Reading adds another input modality in which form, learned representations, and experience interact during recognition.
